extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, mathematical researchers, graduate students, and authors/educators in mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for assessing and presenting mathematical work so it conveys human understanding, opens new questions, connects ideas, and endures; intended for mathematicians writing, reviewing, or teaching research-level mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Does it transfer understanding?
rubrics_metrics.description: Central, recurring criterion in the essay: mathematics is the production of human understanding; proofs and exposition should transfer understanding, not merely establish formal correctness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good exposition identifies which conceptual viewpoints a reader already has and provides the missing ones; evaluate whether the work makes the mathematical ideas accessible to its intended audience. Anti-pattern: a technically correct result that leaves others no closer to grasping the ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof as a social-epistemic act (convincing the community)
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof's role is to convince the relevant mathematical community; proof is thereby a social-epistemic act rather than solely a formal artifact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the argument, presentation, and surrounding explanation will persuade peers who share the community's standards. Consider community norms about acceptable levels of detail, style, and acceptable implicit knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience-appropriateness / standards depend on audience
rubrics_metrics.description: The standard for a 'good proof' depends on what understanding the audience already has.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor exposition to the audience's prior conceptual repertoire; what suffices for experts may be unhelpful for learners, and what aids broad understanding may require more intuition and multiple viewpoints. Scoring should factor in intended readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicative clarity over mere formal completeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal rigor (e.g., machine-checkable proofs, extremely detailed formalization) does not guarantee good communication; such proofs can be poor expository vehicles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value arguments that illuminate despite leaving formal details sketchy, provided they transfer understanding. Anti-patterns: dumping a fully formalized proof or proof-assistant output without intuition, heuristics, or conceptual framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opens new questions (generativity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The best proofs raise more questions than they settle; a valuable piece of work suggests new directions of inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the work spawns natural conjectures, generalizations, or new problems; give credit for enabling future research even when it does not resolve every aspect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connects previously unrelated ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Good work finds and builds connections between topics or viewpoints that were previously unconnected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the paper/unfolded proofs unify disparate concepts or methods, creating bridges that let techniques or intuitions transfer across areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Durability across generations (robustness of conceptual contribution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the work 'survive' future generations of mathematicians who think differently—i.e., remain useful and intelligible when mental frameworks change?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer contributions that provide conceptual frameworks, multiple perspectives, or foundational intuitions that are likely to be assimilated and reused rather than brittle, idiosyncratic constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Raises the field's level (field-elevating impact)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the contribution raises the entire field's level rather than merely adding an isolated theorem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for shifts in perspective, methods, or standards that enable broader progress; count influence on pedagogy, follow-on results, and changed expectations as part of impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multi-modal exposition / multiple conceptual models
rubrics_metrics.description: Exposition should be multi-modal (geometric + algebraic + intuitive + formal); different people understand the same concept via different models (Thurston's derivative example: infinitesimal, symbolic, logical/epsilon-delta, geometric, rate, approximation, microscopic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good papers present several complementary viewpoints to allow readers with different mental models to 'hook' the idea. When possible, give geometric pictures, formal definitions, intuitive narratives, and examples/approximations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicate ways of thinking (heuristics and mental models)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should communicate not just definitions, theorems, and proofs, but also their ways of thinking—heuristics, intuitions, mental images, and strategies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate exposition for inclusion of worked examples, heuristic explanations, motivating stories, and indications of how the author discovered or conceptualizes the results. These elements help others adopt the same lines of thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of speculative, partial, and intuition-driven work
rubrics_metrics.description: Progress often lives in the intermediate zone of conjecture, partial proof, and intuition; treating speculative work as worthless because it is not fully rigorous misses its productive role.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge contributions on their ability to advance understanding and suggest directions even if they contain conjectures or informal arguments. Anti-pattern: an insistence on a sharp 'rigorous vs speculative' divide that dismisses useful intuition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absorbability / teachability (avoid proofs nobody else can understand)
rubrics_metrics.description: Work that is correct but incomprehensible to others can hinder progress; proofs should be absorbable by the intended community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for overly idiosyncratic presentations that prevent others from learning and building on the ideas. Thurston's self-critique (his foliations work being correct but not understood) is an example of the harm done by low absorbability.
